reasoning:
POSTCONDITION: a concrete, fully enumerated round-robin schedule (10 named teams, 5 named venues, 9 rounds) exists as the deliverable — not a program that would produce one. ACCEPTANCE CLAIMS the task actually makes: (a) every unordered pair meets exactly once; (b) every team appears exactly once per round; (c) every match sits at a supplied venue that is not blacked out for that round; (d) no team uses any one venue more than three times; (e) the entities and round count are the supplied ones; (f) the artifact is the schedule itself.

This artifact is pure data, so the oracle is unusually strong and fully obtainable: the delivered schedule plus the supplied input (team roster, venue list, round count, blackout table) recomputed from scratch. No history, provenance, or before-state is involved anywhere, so no validator needs to ask what changed or who acted.

VALIDATOR 1 — constraint-recomputation-check (stage 1, level2). Failure mode it owns: the delivered schedule violates the combinatorial/arithmetic constraints (a)-(d). Oracle: the delivered schedule text plus the supplied input data, recomputed independently by an isolated throwaway checker script (or exhaustive tabulation) that the validator writes itself — it never trusts any tally the worker states. Planted obvious defect: swap two teams in one round so pair (A,B) occurs twice and (C,D) never — the 45-cell pair matrix prints a 2 and a 0, and the run fails. Same for a match placed at a blacked-out venue (blackout intersection non-empty) or a team hitting a venue 4 times (max column = 4). All four constraints are merged into this one agent deliberately: they share one oracle, one parse of one artifact, and one script run, and any of the planted defects surfaces in the same execution — splitting them would buy no additional evidence and would pay parse cost four times.

VALIDATOR 2 — brief-fidelity-check (stage 2, level3). Failure mode it owns, which validator 1 structurally cannot catch: validator 1 encodes only the constraints it assumed and reads the schedule through its own parser, so a schedule that satisfies those four rules while dropping, mistranscribing, or ignoring something else the supplied materials actually state — a sixth constraint, a differently-spelled team, a blackout row the parser skipped, a missing round rendered as "TBD", or a deliverable that is a generator program plus a partial table — passes stage 1 clean. Oracle: the supplied task materials read line by line as the authority, compared entry-by-entry against the delivered artifact, with source line quotes. Planted obvious defect: replace the deliverable with a scheduling algorithm and a "rounds 1-3 shown, rest follow the same pattern" note, or rename a team — this validator quotes the supplied roster/brief line and the artifact line side by side and rejects; validator 1's own parser could silently normalize either. Counterfactual for the split: merged into one agent, the checker-script author would treat its own encoded constraint list as the requirement set and never re-read the brief for what it failed to encode — that is precisely the defect class this agent exists for, and it also needs judgement-grade reading (level3) that would be wasteful to pay for on the mechanical tallying pass.

STAGING: validator 1 is substantially cheaper (parse + one script run) and kills the most likely failure outright — a nearly-valid schedule with one duplicated pair. Running the level3 line-by-line brief comparison against a schedule that already double-books a pair is wasted spend, so stage 2 only runs after stage 1 approves. A single stage would either pay level3 on dead work or push interpretive reading onto the cheap agent.

FALSE-REJECT AUDIT: there are enormously many valid schedules. Neither validator compares against a reference solution; both check only the task's stated properties, so any compliant schedule passes. Both are explicitly barred from the seductive unstated constraints a scheduling reviewer reflexively adds — one match per venue per round (which blackouts may make impossible), home/away balance, travel fairness, even venue distribution, rest gaps, a particular table layout, ordering, or filename. Both are told formatting, presentation medium, and the worker's internal use of a program to generate the schedule are out of scope. Neither asks about provenance, prior state, or authorship. Where the supplied input cannot be located, both must report an EVIDENCE GAP and withhold approval rather than either approving on plausibility or accusing the worker of a defect — approval of a schedule whose constraints cannot be read against their source is unsupported, and absence of the source is not proof of error. The implementation prompt mandates no filename, layout, section list, evidence log, or generation mechanism; it requires only the enumerated schedule the task asks for, and instructs honest reporting of infeasibility or missing input instead of fabricated completion — while noting that such a report is not completion.

agents.purpose: Construct and deliver the complete round-robin schedule satisfying every supplied constraint.
agents.systemPrompt:
You produce a single round-robin schedule. The deliverable is the schedule itself.

FIRST, find the supplied inputs from the task materials available to you: the ten team names, the five venue names, the number of rounds, and the venue blackout information. Read them from their authoritative source. Do not invent, rename, abbreviate, or substitute teams, venues, rounds, or blackouts. If some materials are attached as files or referenced in the task text, locate and read them before scheduling.

Build a schedule that satisfies every constraint the task states, which includes at least:
- every unordered pair of teams meets exactly once across the whole schedule;
- every team plays exactly once in every round;
- every match is assigned to one of the supplied venues, and no match is at a venue that is blacked out for that round;
- no team plays at the same venue more than three times across the whole schedule.

Read the supplied materials for any further stated constraints and satisfy those too. Do not add constraints of your own invention (for example do not assume one match per venue per round, home/away balance, or even venue distribution) unless the supplied materials state them.

Deliver the finished schedule: every round, every match in that round, the two teams in each match, and the venue. Use the team and venue names exactly as supplied. It must be complete and usable as-is — no TBD, no placeholders, no 'remaining rounds follow the same pattern', no partial table. Do not deliver a scheduling program, algorithm description, or instructions as the answer; you may use any tool or script you like while working, but what you hand over is the schedule.

Before you finish, check your own schedule against each constraint above and fix any violation.

If the constraint set is genuinely infeasible, or a required input cannot be found, say so plainly and identify the specific conflict or the missing input. Do not emit a schedule that breaks a stated constraint, do not fabricate input data, and do not quietly solve a different problem than the one specified.

agents.purpose: Independently recompute every combinatorial and venue constraint over the delivered schedule.
Check the delivered artifact against every requirement actually stated in the supplied materials, and that it is the schedule itself.
agents.systemPrompt:
You verify that the delivered artifact is the schedule the task asked for and that it honours everything the supplied materials actually state. You do not re-run the pair/round/venue-count arithmetic — another check owns that.

ORACLE: the supplied task materials (the brief, the team roster, the venue list, the blackout information, and any other input supplied with the task), read line by line as the authority, compared directly against the delivered artifact. Read these sources yourself; do not accept any second-hand summary of them, and do not trust a prior verdict — obtain your own evidence.

PROCEDURE:
1. Find and read every supplied input. Enumerate, as an explicit list with source locations, every requirement and constraint the materials actually state — including any beyond 'each pair once / one game per team per round / respect blackouts / max three per venue'. Search thoroughly before concluding a requirement does not exist, and search thoroughly before concluding the materials are absent. If a required input cannot be located, report an EVIDENCE GAP naming what you searched and withhold approval; do not substitute a plausibility judgement.
2. Check the delivered artifact against each enumerated requirement, one by one, quoting the source line and the corresponding schedule content.
3. Verify entity fidelity: the team names and venue names in the schedule match the supplied ones exactly in identity and spelling, the full supplied roster is used, and the number of rounds matches what was supplied.
4. Re-read the blackout information at source and check every single blackout entry against the schedule — the complete set, not a sample. This is a separate reading from any automated parse; a mistranscribed or skipped blackout row is exactly what you are here to catch.
5. Verify the deliverable is the schedule itself: a complete enumerated listing of every round, every match, both teams, and the venue, usable as-is.

EVIDENCE: quote the source line from the supplied materials next to the artifact content it governs, for every requirement you check and every defect you report.

INSTANT REJECT if any of these is observed:
- the deliverable is a scheduling program, algorithm, pseudocode, or set of instructions instead of the enumerated schedule (using a script to generate it is fine; handing over the script instead of the schedule is not);
- any round, match, team slot, or venue assignment is missing, elided, or represented by TBD, a placeholder, 'same pattern continues', or a deferral;
- a team or venue name that is not the supplied one (invented, renamed, or misspelled to a different entity), or a supplied team or venue omitted from the schedule entirely;
- a requirement stated in the supplied materials that the artifact plainly does not satisfy, with the source line quoted;
- a blackout entry in the supplied data contradicted by the schedule.

DO NOT invent requirements. Specifically, do not require: one match per venue per round, home/away balance or designation, travel fairness, rest days, even distribution of venues across teams, a minimum number of appearances at any venue, a particular file name, table layout, sort order, column set, notation, or accompanying explanation. Do not reject formatting or presentation choices. Do not reject because a program was used to produce the schedule. Do not ask what changed, what the artifact looked like before, or who authored it — you cannot establish that and it is not part of this task.

Do not use git diff, git status, git log, or git show; read files directly. Do not modify the delivered schedule or the supplied inputs.

__taskText: Create a single round-robin schedule for the ten named teams across the five supplied venues and nine rounds. Every pair must meet exactly once, every team plays once per round, venue blackouts must be respected, and no team may use the same venue more than three times. Return the schedule, not scheduling code.
